title: One percent network, seventy-eight percent GPU
subtitle: A slow Teams turn was blamed on the cloud hop; measurement showed the network was about one percent of it and a speech GPU shared with an embedding service was most of the rest, so the compute moved and the cloud stayed

stats.label: round trip between the cloud bridge and the home lab
end of speech to first reply audio on a responsive Teams turn
speech GPU utilisation at peak in the slow window, never below 95
frames validated in a closed-loop call, zero rejects

lede: The Teams voice path crosses a cloud: audio leaves Microsoft's media platform, reaches a Windows bridge on an Azure virtual machine, and crosses an authenticated WebSocket to the voice engine on my own hardware, then back. When a Teams turn took about six seconds from the end of a question to the first sound of the answer, the cloud hop was the obvious suspect. The transport was measured on its own first. The bridge's own numbers were sound. A thirty-minute soak carried 91,643 receive buffers at 50.001 per second with zero stalls, one send stall and no reconnects.
evidence: Performance diagnosis: a slow Teams turn blamed on the cloud hop measured at about one percent network and about seventy-eight percent contended speech GPU.
Latency measurement: per-stage timing of a Teams turn, recognition at 253 ms and synthesis at 4.847 s to first frame, before synthesis moved to a GPU of its own.
Microsoft Teams real-time media: a cloud bridge carrying 91,643 buffers at 50.001 per second with zero stalls and a 65 ms round trip to the home lab.
Closed-loop media validation: 5,859 frames validated in a closed-loop call with zero rejects.
author: Corey James
